title: حِكَايَةُ الْعَاشِقِ وَالْمَعْشُوقِ
titleEn: The Lover and the Beloved, continued
part: Night 126 · The Lover and the Beloved, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 603–605 (Night 126, continuing directly from nights-125), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 126 continues the story that the vizier Dandān tells within the tale of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, the story of the lover, the beloved and the go-between. ʿAzīz goes on with his tale to Tāj al-Mulūk. Held down by the slave-girls of the lady he betrayed by marrying, with her knife sharpened for his throat, he remembers his dead cousin ʿAzīza's two sayings — faithfulness is fair, treachery foul — and they save his life. But the lady will not let him go unmarked: she has him tied and castrates him, cauterises the wound and sends him away, telling him he owes his life to his cousin. The night contains this scene of mutilation, translated as the text gives it. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ السَّادِسَةُ وَالْعِشْرُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-sādisatu wa-al-ʿishrūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the sixth and the twenty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and twenty-sixth night,

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الْوَزِيرَ دَنْدَانَ قَالَ لِضَوْؤِ الْمَكَانِ ثُمَّ إِنَّ الشَّابَّ عَزِيزًا قَالَ لِتَاجِ الْمُلُوكِ فَلَمَّا رَأَيْتُ رُوحِي تَحْتَ يَدِ جَوَارِيهَا وَتَعَفَّرَ خَدِّي بِالتُّرَابِ وَرَأَيْتُهَا تَسُنُّ السِّكِّينَ تَحَقَّقْتُ الْمَوْتَ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-wazīra dandāna qāla li-ḍawʾi al-makāni thumma inna al-shābba ʿazīzan qāla li-tāji al-mulūki fa-lammā raʾaytu rūḥī taḥta yadi jawārīhā wa-taʿaffara khaddī bi-al-turābi wa-raʾaytuhā tasunnu al-sikkīna taḥaqqaqtu al-mawta
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O king the happy, that the vizier Dandān said to Ḍawʾ al-Makān: Then the young-man ʿAzīz said to Tāj al-Mulūk: And when I saw my soul under the hand of her slave-girls, and my cheek was-befouled with the dust, and I saw her whetting the knife, I made-certain-of the death.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the vizier Dandān told Ḍawʾ al-Makān that the young man ʿAzīz said to Tāj al-Mulūk: When I saw myself held down by her slave-girls, my cheek rubbed in the dust, and saw her sharpening the knife, I was sure that I was going to die.
sentences.n: The opening reminds the reader how deep the story is nested: Shahrazād tells the king that Dandān told Ḍawʾ al-Makān that ʿAzīz told Tāj al-Mulūk. li-ḍawʾi: the print spells the name ضوؤ, with the hamza on a wāw, as it does elsewhere; the name is Ḍawʾ al-Makān, “Light of the Place”. raʾaytu rūḥī, “I saw my soul”: rūḥ in the spoken sense “self” — “I saw the state I was in”. bi-al-turāb: bi-, “with”, the dust that grimed his cheek. taḥaqqaqtu al-mawta, “I was certain of death”.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذَلِكَ اسْتَغَثْتُ بِهَا فَلَمْ تَزْدَدْ إِلَّا قَسَاوَةً
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika istaghathtu bihā fa-lam tazdad illā qasāwatan
sentences.l: And at that I sought-help with her, and she did not increase except (in) hardness.
sentences.i: Then I begged her for mercy, but it only made her harder.
sentences.n: istaghathtu bihā, “I cried to her for help”: istaghātha takes bi- for the one appealed to. lam tazdad illā qasāwatan, “she increased only in hardness”: the accusative names what she grew in.

sentences.t: وَأَمَرَتِ الْجَوَارِيَ أَنْ يُكَتِّفْنَنِي فَكَتَّفْنَنِي وَرَمَيْنَنِي عَلَى ظَهْرِي وَجَلَسْنَ عَلَى بَطْنِي وَمَسَكْنَ رَأْسِى
sentences.tr: wa-amarati al-jawāriya an yukattifnanī fa-kattafnanī wa-ramaynanī ʿalā ẓahrī wa-jalasna ʿalā baṭnī wa-masakna raʾsī
sentences.l: And she commanded the slave-girls that they bind-my-arms, and they bound-my-arms, and they threw me on my back, and they sat on my belly, and they held my head.
sentences.i: She ordered the slave-girls to tie my arms behind me, and they tied them, threw me on my back, sat on my belly and held my head.
sentences.n: kattafa, from katif “shoulder”: to tie someone's arms behind his back. The verbs carry the feminine plural ending -na, since the slave-girls do it all.

sentences.t: وَقَامَتْ جَارِيَتَانِ جَلَسَتَا عَلَى أَقْصَابِ رِجْلَايَ وَجَارِيَتَانِ مَسَكَتَا يَدَايَ
sentences.tr: wa-qāmat jāriyatāni jalasatā ʿalā aqṣābi rijlāya wa-jāriyatāni masakatā yadāya
sentences.l: And two slave-girls stood-up (and) sat on the shanks of my two legs, and two slave-girls held my two hands.
sentences.i: Two slave-girls sat on my shins and two held my hands.
sentences.n: rijlāya and yadāya, “my two legs”, “my two hands”: the dual is left in its nominative form -āya after a noun and as an object, where Classical Arabic would write rijlayya and yadayya — the spoken language has one form of the dual for every case. aqṣāb, plural of qaṣaba, “reed”, here the long bones of the shin. masaka, “hold”: the spoken verb, Classical amsaka.

sentences.t: وَقَامَتْ هِيَ وَمَعَهَا جَارِيَتَانِ فَأَمَرَتْهُمَا أَنْ يَضْرِبَانِي فَضَرَبَتَانِي حَتَّى أُغْمِيَ عَلَيَّ وَخَفِيَ صَوْتِي
sentences.tr: wa-qāmat hiya wa-maʿahā jāriyatāni fa-amarathumā an yaḍribānī fa-ḍarabatānī ḥattā ughmiya ʿalayya wa-khafiya ṣawtī
sentences.l: And she stood-up, she, and with her two slave-girls, and she commanded them-two that they beat me, and they-two beat me until it-was-fainted upon me and my voice became-hidden.
sentences.i: Then she got up with two more slave-girls and ordered them to beat me, and they beat me until I fainted and my voice failed.
sentences.n: an yaḍribānī, “that they beat me”: the verb is masculine dual, though two women are meant, where Classical Arabic would write an taḍribānī — spoken usage again; the final -nī is the object “me”. ughmiya ʿalayya, “it was fainted upon me”: the impersonal passive for “I fainted”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا اسْتَفَقْتُ قُلْتُ فِي نَفْسِي إِنَّ مَوْتِي مَذْبُوحًا أَحْسَنُ وَأَهْوَنُ عَلَيَّ مِنْ هَذَا الضَّرْبِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā istafaqtu qultu fī nafsī inna mawtī madhbūḥan aḥsanu wa-ahwanu ʿalayya min hādhā al-ḍarbi
sentences.l: And when I came-to I said in my soul: My dying slaughtered (is) better and easier upon me than this beating.
sentences.i: When I came to, I said to myself, “To die with my throat cut would be better and easier for me than this beating.”
sentences.n: mawtī madhbūḥan, “my dying slaughtered”: the accusative describes the manner of the death.

sentences.t: وَتَذَكَّرْتُ قَوْلَ بِنْتِ عَمِّي فَإِنَّهَا كَانَتْ تَقُولُ لِى كَفَاكَ اللّٰهُ شَرَّهَا
sentences.tr: wa-tadhakkartu qawla binti ʿammī fa-innahā kānat taqūlu lī kafāka allāhu sharrahā
sentences.l: And I remembered the saying of the daughter of my paternal-uncle, for she used to say to me: May God suffice you her evil.
sentences.i: And I remembered what my cousin used to say to me: “May God keep you from her harm.”
sentences.n: kafāka allāhu sharrahā, “may God suffice you (against) her evil”: kafā takes two objects, the person spared and the thing he is spared.

sentences.t: فَصَرَخْتُ وَبَكَيْتُ حَتَّى انْقَطَعَ صَوْتِي وَمَابَقِيَ لِي حِسٌّ وَلَا نَفَسٌ
sentences.tr: fa-ṣarakhtu wa-bakaytu ḥattā inqaṭaʿa ṣawtī wa-mā baqiya lī ḥissun wa-lā nafasun
sentences.l: And I screamed and I wept until my voice was-cut-off, and there did not remain to me sound nor breath.
sentences.i: I screamed and wept until my voice gave out and I had neither voice nor breath left.
sentences.n: mā baqiya lī, “there did not remain to me”: the print runs mā into the verb, as it often does. ḥiss here is “sound, voice” rather than “feeling”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ سَنَّتِ السِّكِّينَ وَقَالَتْ لِلْجَوَارِي اكْشِفْنَ عَنْهُ
sentences.tr: thumma sannati al-sikkīna wa-qālat li-al-jawārī ikshifna ʿanhu
sentences.l: Then she whetted the knife and she said to the slave-girls: Uncover from-him.
sentences.i: Then she sharpened the knife and said to the slave-girls, “Uncover him.”
sentences.n: ikshifna ʿanhu, “uncover (the clothing) from him”: feminine plural imperative.

sentences.t: فَأَلْهَمَنِى الْمَوْلَى أَنْ أَقُولَ الْكَلِمَتَيْنِ اللَّتَيْنِ قَالَتْهُمَا بِنْتُ عَمِّى وَأَوْصَتْنِي بِهِمَا فَقُلْتُ يَاسَيِّدَتِي أَمَا عَلِمْتِ أَنَّ الْوَفَاءَ مَلِيحٌ * وَالْغَدْرَ قَبِيحٌ *
sentences.tr: fa-alhamanī al-mawlā an aqūla al-kalimatayni allatayni qālathumā bintu ʿammī wa-awṣatnī bihimā fa-qultu yā sayyidatī amā ʿalimti anna al-wafāʾa malīḥun * wa-al-ghadra qabīḥun *
sentences.l: And the Lord inspired me that I say the two words which the daughter of my paternal-uncle said and charged me with them, and I said: O my lady, did you not know that faithfulness (is) fine * and the treachery (is) foul? *
sentences.i: Then the Lord put it into my mind to say the two sayings my cousin had spoken and charged me to say, and I said, “My lady, do you not know that faithfulness is fair, and treachery foul?”
sentences.n: al-kalimatayni, “the two words”: the two short rhymed sayings ʿAzīza left him before she died, al-wafāʾu malīḥ / wa-al-ghadru qabīḥ; the print marks the rhyme with its asterisks. awṣatnī bihimā, “she charged me with them”: awṣā takes bi- for what is entrusted. al-mawlā, “the Lord (Master)”, here God.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَتْ ذَلِكَ صَاحَتْ وَقَالَتْ يَرْحَمُكِ اللّٰهُ يَاعَزِيزَةُ اللّٰهُ يُعَوِّضُهَا فِي شَبَابِهَا الْجَنَّةَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿat dhālika ṣāḥat wa-qālat yarḥamuki allāhu yā ʿazīzatu allāhu yuʿawwiḍuhā fī shabābihā al-jannata
sentences.l: And when she heard that she cried-out and said: May God have-mercy-on you, O ʿAzīza! God, may He recompense her for her youth (with) the Garden!
sentences.i: When she heard that, she cried out and said, “God have mercy on you, ʿAzīza! May God give her Paradise in return for her youth!”
sentences.n: She turns from addressing the dead ʿAzīza (yarḥamuki, “may He have mercy on you”, feminine) to speaking of her (yuʿawwiḍuhā, “may He recompense her”) within one breath. ʿawwaḍa X fī Y Z: to give X Z in exchange for Y — Paradise for a youth cut short.

sentences.t: وَاللّٰهِ إِنَّهَا نَفَعَتْكَ فِي حَيَاتِهَا وَبَعْدَ وَفَاتِهَا وَخَلَّصَتْكَ مِنْ يَدِي بِسَبَبِ هَاتَيْنِ الْكَلِمَتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: wa-allāhi innahā nafaʿatka fī ḥayātihā wa-baʿda wafātihā wa-khallaṣatka min yadī bi-sababi hātayni al-kalimatayni
sentences.l: And by God, she benefited you in her life and after her death, and she rescued you from my hand by reason of these two words.
sentences.i: By God, she did you good in her lifetime and after her death, and she has saved you from my hands by means of these two sayings.
sentences.n: bi-sababi, “by reason of”: bi- with sabab, “cause”.

sentences.t: وَلَكِنْ لَا يُمْكِنُ أَتْرُكُكَ هَكَذَا وَلَابُدَّ أَنِّي أَعْمَلُ فِيكَ أَثَرًا لِأَجْلِ نِكَايَةِ تِلْكَ الْعَاهِرَةِ الْمَهْتُوكَةِ الَّتِي حَجَبَتْكَ عَنِّي
sentences.tr: wa-lākin lā yumkinu atrukuka hākadhā wa-lā budda annī aʿmalu fīka atharan li-ajli nikāyati tilka al-ʿāhirati al-mahtūkati allatī ḥajabatka ʿannī
sentences.l: But it is not possible (that) I leave you thus, and there is no escape that I make in you a mark, for the sake of spiting that whore, the shameless, who veiled you from me.
sentences.i: But I cannot let you go like this; I must leave a mark on you, to spite that shameless whore who kept you from me.
sentences.n: lā yumkinu atrukuka, “it is not possible I leave you”: the spoken language drops the an that Classical Arabic needs after yumkinu, and the verb stays indicative. wa-lā budda annī aʿmalu, “and there is no avoiding that I do”. nikāya, “spiting, doing harm to an enemy”. al-mahtūka, “the one whose veil is torn”, i.e. shameless. The insult is aimed at ʿAzīz's wife.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ صَاحَتْ عَلَى الْجَوَارِي وَأَمَرَتْهُنَّ أَنْ يَرْبُطْنَ رِجْلَايَ بِالْحَبْلِ ثُمَّ قَالَتْ لَهُنَّ ارْكَبْنَ عَلَيْهِ فَفَعَلْنَ ذَلِكَ
sentences.tr: thumma ṣāḥat ʿalā al-jawārī wa-amarathunna an yarbuṭna rijlāya bi-al-ḥabli thumma qālat lahunna irkabna ʿalayhi fa-faʿalna dhālika
sentences.l: Then she shouted at the slave-girls and commanded them that they tie my two legs with the rope, then she said to them: Mount upon him! And they did that.
sentences.i: Then she shouted to the slave-girls and ordered them to tie my legs with the rope; then she told them, “Sit on him,” and they did.
sentences.n: ṣāḥat ʿalā, “shouted at, called for”: the spoken idiom. irkabna ʿalayhi, “mount on him”, i.e. hold him down with their weight. rijlāya: the dual again in its one spoken form.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَامَتْ مِنْ عِنْدِي وَأَتَتْ بِطَاجِنٍ مِنْ نُحَاسٍ وَعَلَّقَتْهُ عَلَى كَانُونِ نَارٍ وَصَبَّتْ فِيهِ شِيرَجًا وَقَلَتْ فِيهِ جُبُنًّا وَأَنَا غَائِبٌ عَنِ الدُّنْيَا
sentences.tr: thumma qāmat min ʿindī wa-atat bi-ṭājinin min nuḥāsin wa-ʿallaqathu ʿalā kānūni nārin wa-ṣabbat fīhi shīrajan wa-qalat fīhi jubunnan wa-anā ghāʾibun ʿani al-dunyā
sentences.l: Then she rose from beside me and came with a frying-pan of copper, and she hung it over a brazier of fire, and poured into it sesame-oil, and fried in it cheese, and I (was) absent from the world.
sentences.i: Then she left me, brought a copper pan and hung it over a brazier, poured sesame oil into it and fried cheese in it, while I lay senseless.
sentences.n: atat bi-, “came with”, i.e. brought: the verb chooses the preposition. ṭājin, a shallow pan for frying. shīraj, sesame oil (from Persian). qalat, “she fried”, from qalā. jubunn, “cheese”, one of the word's old forms (the print sets the shadda); the text does not say what they are for; the hot oil at least seems meant for the wound that follows. ghāʾibun ʿani al-dunyā, “absent from the world”: unconscious.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَتَتْ إِلَيَّ وَحَلَّتْ لِبَاسِي وَرَبَطَتْ مَحَاشِمِى بِحَبْلٍ وَأَمْسَكَتْهُ وَنَاوَلَتْهُ لِجَارِيَتَيْنِ وَقَالَتْ لَهُمَا جُرَّا الْحَبْلَ فَجَرَّتَاهُ
sentences.tr: thumma atat ilayya wa-ḥallat libāsī wa-rabaṭat maḥāshimī bi-ḥablin wa-amsakathu wa-nāwalathu li-jāriyatayni wa-qālat lahumā jurrā al-ḥabla fa-jarratāhu
sentences.l: Then she came to me and untied my drawers, and she tied my private-parts with a rope, and she held it and handed it to two slave-girls, and she said to them-two: Pull the rope! And they-two pulled it.
sentences.i: Then she came to me, undid my drawers, tied a rope round my private parts, took hold of it and handed it to two slave-girls, and told them, “Pull the rope.” They pulled it,
sentences.n: libās here is the drawers, the garment tied at the waist with a cord. maḥāshim, “private parts”, plural of maḥsham. nāwalathu li-, “handed it to”: li- marks the one who receives.

sentences.t: فَغُشِيَ عَلَيَّ وَصِرْتُ مِنْ شِدَّةِ الْأَلَمِ فِي دُنْيَا غَيْرِ هَذِهِ الدُّنْيَا
sentences.tr: fa-ghushiya ʿalayya wa-ṣirtu min shiddati al-alami fī dunyā ghayri hādhihi al-dunyā
sentences.l: And it-was-swooned upon me, and I became, from the violence of the pain, in a world other than this world.
sentences.i: and I swooned, and from the force of the pain I was in another world than this.
sentences.n: ghushiya ʿalayya, “it was swooned upon me”: another impersonal passive for fainting.

sentences.t: وَجَاءَتْ بِمُوسَى مِنْ حَدِيدٍ وَقَطَعَتْ ذَكَرِي وَبَقِيتُ مِثْلَ الْمَرْأَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-jāʾat bi-mūsā min ḥadīdin wa-qaṭaʿat dhakarī wa-baqītu mithla al-marʾati
sentences.l: And she came with a razor of iron and cut-off my penis, and I remained like the woman.
sentences.i: She brought an iron razor and cut off my penis, and I was left like a woman.
sentences.n: jāʾat bi-, “came with”, brought. mūsā, “razor”. dhakar, “male member”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ كَوَتْ مَوْضِعَ الْقَطْعِ وَكَبَسَتْهُ بِذَرُورٍ وَأَنَا مُغْمًى عَلَيَّ
sentences.tr: thumma kawat mawḍiʿa al-qaṭʿi wa-kabasathu bi-dharūrin wa-anā mughman ʿalayya
sentences.l: Then she cauterised the place of the cutting and pressed it with a powder, and I (was) fainted-upon.
sentences.i: Then she cauterised the place of the cut and packed it with a powder, while I lay unconscious.
sentences.n: kawā, “burn, cauterise”: probably with the hot oil, a common way of stanching an amputation. kabasa, “press, pack”; dharūr, a dry medicinal powder sprinkled on a wound. mughman ʿalayya, “fainted upon”: the passive participle of ughmiya ʿalā.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَفَقْتُ كَانَ الدَّمُ قَدِ انْقَطَعَ فَأَمَرَتِ الْجَوَارِيَ أَنْ يُحَلِّلْنَنِي فَأَسْقَتْنِي قَدَحَ شَرَابٍ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā afaqtu kāna al-damu qadi inqaṭaʿa fa-amarati al-jawāriya an yuḥallilnanī fa-asqatnī qadaḥa sharābin
sentences.l: And when I came-to, the blood had been cut-off, and she commanded the slave-girls that they untie me, and she gave-me-to-drink a cup of drink.
sentences.i: When I came to, the bleeding had stopped. She ordered the slave-girls to untie me, and she gave me a cup of wine to drink.
sentences.n: yuḥallilnanī, “that they untie me”: form II of ḥalla. sharāb, “drink”, in the Nights usually wine.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَتْ لِي رُحِ الْآنَ لِلَّتِي تَزَوَّجْتَ بِهَا وَبَخِلْتَ عَلَيَّ بِلَيْلَةٍ وَاحِدَةٍ
sentences.tr: thumma qālat lī ruḥi al-āna li-allatī tazawwajta bihā wa-bakhilta ʿalayya bi-laylatin wāḥidatin
sentences.l: Then she said to me: Go now to the-one whom you married, and you begrudged me one night!
sentences.i: Then she said to me, “Go now to the woman you married — you who grudged me a single night.
sentences.n: ruḥ, “go!”: the spoken imperative of rāḥa. tazawwajta bihā, “you married her”: the verb takes bi- for the spouse. bakhilta ʿalayya bi-, “you were stingy towards me with”: bakhila takes ʿalā for the one refused and bi- for the thing withheld.

sentences.t: رَحِمَ اللّٰهُ بِنْتَ عَمِّكَ الَّتِي هِيَ سَبَبُ نَجَاتِكَ وَلَمْ تُبِحْ سِرَّهَا
sentences.tr: raḥima allāhu binta ʿammika allatī hiya sababu najātika wa-lam tubiḥ sirrahā
sentences.l: May God have-mercy-on the daughter of your paternal-uncle, who she (is) the cause of your rescue, and she did not divulge her secret.
sentences.i: God have mercy on your cousin, who is the reason you are saved, and who never gave away her secret.
sentences.n: lam tubiḥ sirrahā, “she did not divulge her secret”: ʿAzīza kept her own love hidden to the end and told him only what would protect him.

sentences.t: وَلَوْلَا أَنَّكَ أَسْمَعْتَنِي كَلِمَتَيْهَا لَكُنْتُ ذَبَحْتُكَ فَاذْهَبْ فِي هَذِهِ السَّاعَةِ لِمَنْ تَشْتَهِي
sentences.tr: wa-lawlā annaka asmaʿtanī kalimatayhā la-kuntu dhabaḥtuka fa-idhhab fī hādhihi al-sāʿati li-man tashtahī
sentences.l: And were-it-not that you made-me-hear her two words, I would have slaughtered you; so go at this hour to whom you desire.
sentences.i: If you had not let me hear her two sayings, I would have cut your throat. So go this very hour to whomever you like.
sentences.n: la-kuntu dhabaḥtuka, “I would have slaughtered you”: la- opens the answer to lawlā. li-man, “to whom(ever)”: li- of direction.

sentences.t: وَأَنَا مَا كَانَ لِي عِنْدَكَ غَيْرُالَّذِي قَطَعْتُهُ وَالْآنَ مَابَقِيَ لِي عِنْدَكَ شَيْءٌ وَلَالِي فِيكَ رَغْبَةٌ وَلَاحَاجَةَ لِي بِكَ
sentences.tr: wa-anā mā kāna lī ʿindaka ghayru alladhī qaṭaʿtuhu wa-al-āna mā baqiya lī ʿindaka shayʾun wa-lā lī fīka raghbatun wa-lā ḥājata lī bika
sentences.l: And I, there was not for me with you other-than that-which I cut-off, and now there does not remain for me with you a thing, nor to me in you a desire, and no need to me for you.
sentences.i: As for me, there was nothing I wanted from you but what I have cut off; now there is nothing of yours left that I want. I have no desire for you and no use for you.
sentences.n: The print runs several words together here: ghayru alladhī, mā baqiya, wa-lā lī, wa-lā ḥājata. ḥājata lī bika, “need to me for you”: ḥāja takes bi- for what is needed.

sentences.t: فَقُمْ وَمَلِّسْ عَلَى رَأْسِكَ وَتَرَحَّمْ عَلَى بِنْتِ عَمِّكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qum wa-mallis ʿalā raʾsika wa-taraḥḥam ʿalā binti ʿammika
sentences.l: So stand-up, and smooth over your head, and call-mercy upon the daughter of your paternal-uncle!
sentences.i: So get up, stroke your head, and pray for God's mercy on your cousin.”
sentences.n: The print spells raʾs without hamza, راس, as it often does. mallis ʿalā raʾsika, “smooth (your hand) over your head”: a colloquial phrase not found in the classical dictionaries; malasa/mallasa is “to smooth, stroke”, and the sense is perhaps “console yourself (with what you have)” — the reading is uncertain. taraḥḥam ʿalā, “ask God's mercy upon”, pray for the dead.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ رَفَصَتْنِي بِرِجْلِهَا فَقُمْتُ وَمَا قَدَرْتُ أَنْ أَمْشِيَ فَتَمَشَّيْتُ قَلِيلًا قَلِيلًا حَتَّى وَصَلْتُ إِلَى الْبَابِ
sentences.tr: thumma rafaṣatnī bi-rijlihā fa-qumtu wa-mā qadartu an amshiya fa-tamashshaytu qalīlan qalīlan ḥattā waṣaltu ilā al-bābi
sentences.l: Then she kicked me with her foot, and I stood-up and I was not able to walk, so I made-my-way little by little until I reached to the door.
sentences.i: Then she kicked me, and I got up. I could not walk, so I edged forward little by little until I reached the door.
sentences.n: rafaṣa, “kick”: the spoken form of Classical rafasa, with ṣ for s. bi-rijlihā, “with her foot”: bi- of the instrument. tamashshā, “walk slowly, make one's way”.

sentences.t: فَوَجَدْتُهُ مَفْتُوحًا فَرَمَيْتُ نَفْسِى فِيهِ وَأَنَا غَائِبٌ عَنِ الْوُجُودِ
sentences.tr: fa-wajadtuhu maftūḥan fa-ramaytu nafsī fīhi wa-anā ghāʾibun ʿani al-wujūdi
sentences.l: And I found it opened, and I threw my soul into it, and I (was) absent from existence.
sentences.i: I found it open and threw myself through it, half out of my senses.
sentences.n: ghāʾibun ʿani al-wujūd, “absent from existence”: barely conscious. The door is his own house's, as what follows shows.

sentences.t: وَإِذَابِزَوْجَتِي خَرَجَتْ وَحَمَلَتْنِي وَأَدْخَلَتْنِى الْقَاعَةَ فَوَجَدَتْنِي مِثْلَ الْمَرْأَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-idhā bi-zawjatī kharajat wa-ḥamalatnī wa-adkhalatnī al-qāʿata fa-wajadatnī mithla al-marʾati
sentences.l: And behold, (there was) my wife; she came-out and carried me and made-me-enter the hall, and she found me like the woman.
sentences.i: And there was my wife: she came out, carried me in to the hall, and found me like a woman.
sentences.n: wa-idhā bi-zawjatī, “and behold, my wife”: after idhā of surprise, bi- only marks what appears; the print runs the three words together.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنِّي نِمْتُ وَاسْتَغْرَقْتُ فِى النَّوْمِ فَلَمَّا قُمْتُ وَصَحَوْتُ وَجَدْتُ نَفْسِي مَرْمِيًّا عَلَى بَابِ الْبُسْتَانِ
sentences.tr: thumma innī nimtu wa-istaghraqtu fī al-nawmi fa-lammā qumtu wa-ṣaḥawtu wajadtu nafsī marmiyyan ʿalā bābi al-bustāni
sentences.l: Then I slept and was-drowned in the sleep; and when I rose and woke, I found my soul thrown at the door of the garden.
sentences.i: Then I fell asleep and slept deeply, and when I got up and woke, I found myself lying thrown down at the garden gate.
sentences.n: istaghraqa fī al-nawm, “to be sunk in sleep”. The print gives the sequence so: carried into the hall, then waking at the garden gate; it is translated as it stands.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: Morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent, leaving the permitted speech.
